paras: The lynching of Sank Majors took place at Waco, Texas, early on August 8, 1905, when a large mob broke into the county jail, seized Majors, a young Black prisoner, and hanged him from a bridge over the Brazos River. Majors had been convicted of criminally assaulting a white woman and sentenced to death, but a judge had granted him a new trial three days earlier. Many white editorials blamed the court rather than the mob, and a Black man who criticized the lynching was flogged in the county.

According to a Waco special to the San Antonio Daily Light, Majors was charged with assaulting, beating and stabbing Mrs. B. Robert of Golinda on July 11, after a quarrel with "Robert" over crossing a piece of land. Mobs followed his trail for nearly two weeks before his capture at Lockhart, and Golinda residents promised to let the law take its course. Judge Surratt of the Nineteenth district court opened the trial on August 2, and the next day the jury returned a guilty verdict in three minutes and fixed the punishment at death. On August 5 Surratt granted a new trial, which the Associated Press said would keep the appeals court from revising the sentence on a technicality.

The mob gathered at the jail late on August 7 and surrounded the courthouse and jail. Its leaders battered the doors with sledge hammers and rams while Sheriff George Tilley "remonstrated" with them. Tilley, the jailer, the deputies and Mayor Jim Baker were made prisoners or overpowered, and five doors were smashed before Majors's cell was reached.

The mob first intended to burn Majors, and a Houston dispatch to the St. Louis Republic said the mounted men had brought oil and debated for nearly an hour before a vote chose the rope. Wire reports said the mob heard Majors's confession before hanging him from the new Brazos bridge on Washington street at about 2 a.m. The body was left hanging for about an hour while the men, described as "friends and neighbors of the woman" from the Golinda section, rode out of the city.

Governor Lanham announced an investigation and refused to pay the reward for Majors's arrest because the execution was not according to law; county citizens raised it for the officers instead. No report of an inquest, arrests or indictments of mob members appears in the coverage.

On the night of August 9 about twenty men flogged Jim Lawyer, a Black man near Bruceville, for condemning "the whites for lynching Sank Majors," and he left the next morning. A Waco report said white residents would not disturb Black residents "as long as the negroes keep their tongues and places," and officers later permitted no "incendiar remarks" among them.

Headlines included "NEGRO LYNCHED AT WACO" on the Associated Press account and "TWO THOUSAND LYNCH HIM" on a Fort Worth wire. Texas papers framed the hanging as vengeance, the Waxahachie Daily Light headlining "A Brutal Assault Upon a Defenseless Woman Avenged by a Mob of Neighbors" and the San Antonio Daily Light giving court delays as "the reasons assigned."

White editorial comment largely shifted the blame to the court. The Montgomery Advertiser's "Trifling With Justice" said "the first trifling with justice was in the courthouse," and the Brooklyn Eagle, the Wheeling Register and the Arizona Republican's "Inviting the Mob" made the same argument. The Omaha Bee and a lawyer's letter to the Advertiser, which called every lyncher guilty of murder, dissented.

The Black press coverage found was brief. The Cleveland Gazette printed a two-sentence wire item in a general-news column, naming the victim "Haig Majors," without comment. In the Muskogee Cimeter, editor W. H. Twine set the Waco hanging beside a burning at Sulphur Springs, wrote "Mind you that is Lynch law," and declared "No mob law in ours."

Estimates of the mob ran from three hundred (San Antonio Daily Light) and six hundred (Associated Press) to fifteen hundred (Houston dispatch) and two thousand (Fort Worth and Waxahachie reports). The San Antonio paper said the woman's husband asked that Majors be hanged rather than burned, while the Houston dispatch described a vote; the confession appears only as the mob's account.

reader.title: Lynching of Sank Majors
bases: A crowd broke into the county jail at Waco, took out a prisoner awaiting retrial and hanged him from a bridge (A5, A7, A9).

Majors was hanged by a mob numbered from 300 to 2,000 that overpowered the sheriff and broke into the jail (A5, A7, A9); the papers give impatience with court delay after his conviction for criminal assault as the reason (A7, A22).
The AP wire, a Waco special to the San Antonio Daily Light, a Waxahachie report, a Fort Worth wire and a Houston dispatch agree on the jail break and hanging from a bridge (A5, A7, A8, A9, A15).

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: About 600 mounted citizens surrounded the jail at 2 a.m., made prisoners of the sheriff and deputies, heard Majors's confession and hanged him from the new bridge.

accounts.label: Waco special to the San Antonio Daily Light
accounts.gist: An armed mob of 300 battered the jail doors for half an hour, halted on the square to burn Majors, hanged him at the husband's request, and rode out; delay in the courts was the reason given.

accounts.label: Waxahachie Daily Light
accounts.gist: About 2,000 from the Golinda section formed at 11:45, smashed five doors, overpowered mayor and sheriff, were dissuaded from burning and hanged Majors from the Washington street bridge.

accounts.label: Houston dispatch (St. Louis Republic)
accounts.gist: 500 mounted men and 1,000 on foot brought oil to burn Majors; after an hour's debate a vote chose hanging, and he was hanged from the railroad bridge.

accounts.label: Black press brief
accounts.gist: A two-sentence summary of the wire: 600 citizens, 'Haig Majors, colored', confession, hanged from a bridge.

framing.detail: AP headline 'NEGRO LYNCHED AT WACO. A Texas Mob Hanged Confessed Criminal'; Fort Worth wire 'TWO THOUSAND LYNCH HIM'.
Waxahachie Daily Light: 'A Brutal Assault Upon a Defenseless Woman Avenged by a Mob of Neighbors'; mob 'preserved perfect discipline'.
Montgomery Advertiser 'Trifling With Justice', Brooklyn Eagle, Wheeling Register and Arizona Republican blamed the court's new trial for the lynching.
Omaha Bee said the usual defense of mobs failed here; a lawyer's letter to the Advertiser said lynchers were guilty of murder.
Fort Worth Record (via Ardmoreite) attacked 'gabby negroes' who discussed the Waco lynching.
Cleveland Gazette ran the wire facts in a general-news column without comment.
Muskogee Cimeter: 'Mind you that is Lynch law'; 'No mob law in ours'.

record_check.dossier: One victim, Sank Majors; 'Haig Majors' is the Cleveland Gazette's rendering of the same man
Charged with criminally assaulting Mrs. B. Robert near Golinda July 11; convicted Aug. 3 and sentenced to death; granted a new trial Aug. 5 and awaiting retrial
No beating of Majors by the mob is reported (the beating in the papers is the assault he was charged with); acts were siege of the jail, seizure and hanging
Unnamed mounted and armed white men said to be friends and neighbors of the woman from the Golinda section

record_check.record: about a crowd of several hundred ... after taking his confession
record_check.dossier: Crowd estimates run from 300 to 2,000; the confession is the mob's and wire's claim
County not named in the opened articles (county jail at Waco); spelling should be McLennan if kept
In the aftermath Jim Lawyer was flogged near Bruceville for condemning the lynching (a separate reprisal)
